patient.name: Sofia Marchetti
patient.complaint: Itchy raised rash that moves around her body, for 2 days
background: Asthma and eczema as a child; hay fever every summer
Sore throat and cold last week; took ibuprofen for it
Trainee solicitor in Islington; no regular medicines

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with itchy, transient wheals that come and go within 24 hours, often after a virus, food or NSAID. The duration (under or over 6 weeks) and airway signs change the answer.

points: Sofia, 27, woke yesterday with **intensely itchy** raised blotches.
Each blotch fades within hours, then new ones appear elsewhere.
Last week: a cold; she took **ibuprofen** for 3 days.
No lip swelling, no wheeze, no breathing difficulty.

steps.lead: Itchy, raised, short-lived wheals are **urticaria**: histamine from skin mast cells making small vessels leak.
Sofia's childhood asthma, eczema and hay fever make her **atopic**, which raises the risk.

points: Pink, raised **wheals** on her trunk and arms.
Well-defined edges, some **merging**, a few with pale centres.
Pen marks drawn around two wheals: gone by the end of clinic.
No blisters, scale or bruising left behind.

steps.lead: Sofia's lesions are classic: **well-defined, erythematous, serpiginous** borders with central clearing, coming and going.

visual.title: How long one wheal lasts
visual.label: Sofia ~4 h
visual.caption: Each wheal in urticaria clears within 24 hours without marks. A lesion that lasts longer or leaves bruising is not simple urticaria.

steps.lead: Sofia has two triggers in the notes: a **viral infection** and an **NSAID** (ibuprofen).
Two days of wheals after a virus: this is **acute urticaria** (under 6 weeks). If it carries on past 6 weeks it becomes chronic.

steps.q: Which new finding would make Sofia an emergency?
o: Stridor and a BP of 80/50 mmHg
steps.r: Wheeze, **stridor**, **hypotension** or airway swelling means progression to **anaphylaxis**: IM adrenaline, not antihistamines.

steps.lead: Sofia's itch is wrecking her sleep. She must know the red flags of **anaphylaxis** and to call 999.

steps.text: **Angioedema alone** (no wheals) in someone on an **ACE inhibitor** is bradykinin-mediated, not histamine: antihistamines will not help. Always check the drug history.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' where acute urticaria needs none (clinical diagnosis), while chronic or atypical urticaria gets FBC, CRP or ESR and TFTs.

steps.q: Sofia has acute urticaria with an obvious trigger. Which investigation does she need?
o: None: it is a clinical diagnosis
steps.r: Urticaria is a **clinical diagnosis**. Acute urticaria with a clear trigger needs no tests.

steps.lead: Sofia's history and the wheals themselves are the diagnosis. **No routine tests** today.

points: Cetirizine helps, but the wheals keep coming back.
**Eight weeks** later she returns, still having wheals most days.
Ibuprofen has been avoided since the first visit.
She also feels tired and has gained 3 kg.

visual.title: Weeks of recurrent wheals
visual.label: Sofia 8 weeks
visual.caption: Past 6 weeks with no trigger: chronic (spontaneous) urticaria, so now check bloods.

steps.lead: Sofia's urticaria is now **chronic**, so she gets **FBC, CRP/ESR and TFTs**.

steps.title: Sofia's bloods at 8 weeks
steps.text: Normal inflammatory markers, but autoimmune hypothyroidism: the classic association of chronic urticaria.
Chronic urticaria is linked to **autoimmune thyroid disease**. That is why TFTs are on the list.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' with oral non-sedating antihistamine (cetirizine) first line, a short course of oral prednisolone for severe cases, a higher antihistamine dose for chronic disease, and omalizumab when refractory.

steps.title: Treatment ladder for urticaria
nodes: Severe and not responding: short course oral prednisolone
steps.caption: Anaphylaxis is a different pathway: IM adrenaline.

steps.q: What is first-line treatment for Sofia's acute urticaria?
steps.r: A **non-sedating antihistamine** such as cetirizine, plus avoiding the trigger. Adrenaline is only for anaphylaxis.

steps.lead: Sofia stops ibuprofen and starts **cetirizine** each morning. For her sleepless nights, **chlorphenamine** at night.
If Sofia's wheals had been severe and unresponsive, a **short oral prednisolone** course would be added alongside cetirizine.

points: At 8 weeks: chronic urticaria, still on standard-dose cetirizine.
Cetirizine dose increased; she keeps a wheal diary.

steps.lead: Sofia's symptoms persist, so her **antihistamine dose is increased**: the standard step in chronic urticaria.

visual.title: Sofia's weekly urticaria activity score (UAS7)
visual.caption: Higher-dose antihistamine helped a little; omalizumab from week 12 settled it.

steps.lead: Still poorly controlled at week 12, Sofia is referred to a specialist and starts **omalizumab**.

steps.text: Do not jump to oral steroids as maintenance for chronic urticaria. Steroids are a **short rescue course**; long-term control comes from higher-dose antihistamine, then omalizumab.

steps.lead: Sofia's ladder follows the **BSACI** guideline on urticaria and angioedema.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the mechanism of a wheal (mast cell histamine), why angioedema is deeper, why chronic urticaria is autoimmune, and how antihistamines and omalizumab work.

steps.lead: Sofia's wheals come from **mast cells in the superficial dermis** releasing histamine.

steps.title: From trigger to wheal
nodes: Mast cell degranulation in the dermis

steps.lead: If the same process ran deeper, Sofia would get **angioedema**: diffuse swelling of the lips, eyelids or tongue.
Sofia's chronic disease had no trigger because **autoantibodies against FcεRI or IgE** fire her mast cells, which fits her thyroid autoimmunity.

steps.q: Why does cetirizine cause less drowsiness than chlorphenamine?
o: It crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly
steps.r: Non-sedating H1 antihistamines block **H1 receptors** without significant **CNS penetration**.

steps.lead: Cetirizine blocks **H1 receptors**; omalizumab, an **anti-IgE** antibody, lowered Sofia's free IgE and FcεRI expression.

mcq.r: Each wheal lasts **under 24 hours**; longer suggests urticarial vasculitis.

o: Recurrent wheals for 6 weeks or more

mcq.r: Wheeze, **stridor, hypotension**, airway swelling or collapse are anaphylaxis.

mcq.q: What is the gold-standard diagnosis of urticaria?
Which tests are used in chronic or atypical urticaria?

mcq.r: **Cetirizine, loratadine or fexofenadine** plus trigger avoidance.

mcq.q: Which drug is used at night if itch disturbs sleep?

o: Mast cell histamine release increasing vascular permeability
T cell infiltration of the epidermis

glossary.Urticaria: Itchy, raised, short-lived wheals (hives) caused by histamine release in the skin.
glossary.Wheal: A raised, pale or red, itchy swelling of the skin that fades within 24 hours.
glossary.Angioedema: Deeper swelling of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, typically lips, eyelids and tongue.
glossary.Acute urticaria: Urticaria lasting less than 6 weeks, often triggered by infection, food or drugs.
glossary.Chronic urticaria: Recurrent wheals on most days for 6 weeks or more, usually with no identifiable trigger.
glossary.Chronic spontaneous urticaria: Chronic urticaria with no external trigger, often driven by autoantibodies against mast cells.
glossary.Mast cell: Tissue immune cell full of histamine granules that it releases when activated.
glossary.Degranulation: Release of a cell's stored granules, such as histamine from mast cells.
glossary.Histamine: Mediator that dilates vessels, makes capillaries leak and causes itch.
glossary.Atopy: Inherited tendency to allergic disease such as asthma, eczema and hay fever.
glossary.Central clearing: Paler centre to a lesion with a red edge.
glossary.Anaphylaxis: Severe, life-threatening allergic reaction with airway, breathing or circulation compromise.
glossary.Stridor: High-pitched noisy breathing from upper airway narrowing.
glossary.Urticarial vasculitis: Inflamed vessels causing wheal-like lesions that last over 24 hours and leave bruising.
glossary.NSAIDs: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen; a common urticaria trigger.
glossary.Cetirizine: Non-sedating H1 antihistamine; first-line for urticaria.
glossary.Loratadine: Non-sedating H1 antihistamine used first line for urticaria.
glossary.Fexofenadine: Non-sedating H1 antihistamine used first line for urticaria.
glossary.Chlorphenamine: Sedating H1 antihistamine, used at night when itch disturbs sleep.
glossary.H1 receptor: Histamine receptor on vessels and nerves that drives vasodilation, leak and itch.
glossary.Prednisolone: Oral corticosteroid; a short course is second-line for severe urticaria.
glossary.Omalizumab: Anti-IgE monoclonal antibody used for refractory chronic urticaria.
glossary.IgE: Antibody that binds mast cells and triggers degranulation in allergy.
glossary.FcεRI: High-affinity IgE receptor on mast cells; a target of autoantibodies in chronic urticaria.
glossary.TFTs: Thyroid function tests: TSH and free T4.
glossary.Anti-TPO antibodies: Thyroid peroxidase antibodies, a marker of autoimmune thyroid disease.
glossary.UAS7: Urticaria activity score over 7 days (0 to 42), tracking wheals and itch.
glossary.BSACI: British Society for Allergy and Clinical Immunology, which publishes UK urticaria guidance.
glossary.Bradykinin: Vasoactive peptide behind ACE inhibitor angioedema; not blocked by antihistamines.
glossary.Dermographism: Wheals raised along lines where the skin has been stroked or scratched.

technique.stem: A 24 year old woman has a 3 day history of an intensely itchy rash. She had a viral sore throat last week. Individual raised red lesions appear on her trunk and limbs, change shape and fade within a few hours, leaving no mark. She has asthma and hay fever. There is no lip swelling or wheeze.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A rash diagnosis: look at the time course of each lesion and of the whole illness.

clues: change shape and fade within a few hours
steps.x: Itchy transient wheals, post-viral trigger, atopy, 3 days only.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Acute urticaria** (under 6 weeks).

elim: Chronic needs 6 weeks or more.
Erythema multiforme has fixed target lesions lasting days.
Pityriasis rosea has a herald patch and scaly ovals lasting weeks.
Vasculitic lesions last over 24 hours and leave bruising.

steps.x: **A.** Rule: wheals under 24 h + under 6 weeks + trigger = acute urticaria.

practice.stem: A 19 year old man has a 2 day history of an itchy rash after a cold. Raised pink lesions with pale centres appear on his trunk, merge, and disappear within hours, only to appear elsewhere. He has eczema. There is no lip swelling or wheeze. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Itchy, migrating wheals that resolve within hours after a viral illness in an atopic man is acute urticaria. Erythema multiforme lesions are fixed targets lasting days.

steps.x: Diagnosis of an itchy rash.
Transient, migrating wheals; post-viral; atopic; short history.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Acute urticaria.**

elim: Contact dermatitis is fixed, eczematous and at the contact site.
Target lesions that stay for days.
Scaly drop-like plaques that persist.
Burrows, finger webs, worse at night, not migrating wheals.

steps.x: **A.** Rule: lesions that move and vanish within hours = urticaria.

practice.stem: A 42 year old woman has had itchy wheals on most days for 4 months. Each wheal fades within 12 hours without bruising. She cannot identify any trigger. She is otherwise well, with no joint pain or fever. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Recurrent wheals for 6 weeks or more, each under 24 hours, no trigger, no systemic symptoms and normal labs is chronic spontaneous urticaria. Urticarial vasculitis lesions last over 24 hours and bruise.

steps.x: Diagnosis: count the weeks.
Over 6 weeks, transient wheals, no trigger, no systemic features, normal labs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chronic spontaneous urticaria.**

elim: Acute is under 6 weeks.
Hereditary angioedema causes swelling without wheals.

Vasculitic lesions last over 24 hours and leave bruising.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: 6 weeks or more, no trigger, normal labs = chronic urticaria.

practice.stem: A 25 year old woman has itchy, raised wheals 20 minutes after a wasp sting. A skin biopsy taken for research shows dermal oedema with dilated superficial vessels. She has no angioedema, wheeze or hypotension.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her wheals?
o: Deposition of immune complexes in the epidermis
Mast cell degranulation releasing histamine in the superficial dermis
practice.e: Urticaria is caused by mast cell degranulation in the superficial dermis; histamine causes vasodilation and increased capillary permeability, producing itchy raised wheals.
